issues.item: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: For physical abuse by a romantic partner, the threat profile is centered on generalized danger from strangers, while the appraisals are centered on bodily damage/shame and permanent emotional change. This is not impossible, but as the only represented components it is clinically hard to integrate into a single coherent profile of partner abuse without any partner-specific or trauma-linked threat content.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Within the formulation, the only active links are between Negative Appraisals and Threat, so these two nodes should strongly cohere. Here the negative appraisals imply consequences focused on the body and self after intimate physical abuse, but the threat item 'threat from strangers approaching me' points to a different danger representation that is not reflected in the appraisals. That weakens the expected tight appraisal-threat coupling.

vignette:
Mereana was 80 years old when she finally agreed to come in for help, a small, sturdy Māori woman who had spent most of her life working as a welder and still carried herself with the practical economy of someone used to heat, weight, and metal. She had been married for many years, but the trauma she spoke about dated back to a period when a romantic partner had beaten her repeatedly and unpredictably, leaving her to live in a state of constant caution. She described that time in plain, unadorned terms at first, then with more force as the memories became less distant: being grabbed hard enough to bruise, shoved into walls, and made to fear the sound of footsteps in a hallway or a door opening too sharply. What stayed with her most was not one single assault but the sense that danger could arrive without warning in the very place that was supposed to be private and safe.

After those episodes, Mereana noticed that her nights changed. She began taking a long time to fall asleep, lying rigid and listening to every creak in the house. Even after she did drift off, she would wake in the dark and immediately check whether she was safe, sometimes sitting up and scanning the room before she could remember where she was. She kept a light on more often than not and would make quiet rounds through the house, touching the locks on the doors and looking into the hallway before settling again. Even at home, where she had spent years trying to make herself feel settled, she said she remained on guard. A sudden noise in another room, a car passing outside late at night, or the house going unusually still could bring on the same tightening in her chest and the same alertness she had known during the abuse, as if her body were still waiting for the next blow.

Her welding work had once given her a sense of competence and order, but over time she became more protective in that environment too. The daily routines of the workshop - the clang of metal, the sparks, the sharp sounds of tools dropped on a bench - could leave her tense and watchful, and she found herself paying close attention to anyone coming up behind her. She did not describe stopping work entirely, but she had become more guarded in how she moved through her days, especially in enclosed spaces where she could not easily see what was approaching. At home, the same vigilance continued in a quieter form: she checked windows, listened hard at night, and preferred to know exactly who was in each room before she relaxed even slightly. Over the weeks and months after the assaults, these habits settled into her life and made her feel less and less able to rest.

Alongside this ongoing alertness, Mereana had come to believe that the violence had done lasting damage to her body itself. She said, with a flat certainty that was painful to hear, that her body had been permanently damaged by what happened. She did not speak only about bruises or old injuries, but about a deeper sense that something in her had been altered beyond repair. She said she could no longer trust her own body, because it felt unreliable to her now, as though it might fail her without warning or betray her by reacting too strongly or not strongly enough. This mistrust coloured ordinary experiences: if she felt tired, sore, or shaky, she was quick to read it as proof that the harm had stayed inside her. She watched herself closely, aware of every physical sensation, and that close attention left her feeling older than her years.

She also said that she would never be able to feel normal emotions again. The words came slowly, but once spoken they seemed fixed in place. Mereana described herself as emotionally changed, less able to access the kind of warmth, ease, or spontaneous feeling she remembered from earlier in life. At times she seemed disappointed by her own flatness, as if she were measuring herself against a version of herself that no longer existed. The loss was not dramatic in the way the assaults had been, but it was deeply personal to her, and she seemed to regard it as another enduring injury. Even now, when nothing immediate was wrong, she could not fully settle into comfort. She remained watchful in her own house, woke during the night to check whether she was safe, and often began the day already tired from broken sleep.

By the time she sought help, these experiences had become part of how she organised her life, and their effects were noticeable in her marriage and daily routine. She had grown weary of being startled and of feeling as though she had to keep proving to herself that she was secure. What brought her in was not a single crisis but the accumulation of exhausted nights and the growing fear that she would never again feel like herself in her body or in her emotions. She was most afraid that the sense of permanent damage was true, and most hoping, however cautiously, that talking might help her understand why safety still felt so fragile even now, in her own home.
